line: Morning. Frank DeLuca. I've got the hardware store on Fifth, DeLuca's, next to the bank. I don't think we've met?
choice1: I'm {playerName}. I'm pretty new around here.

line: Welcome. If you rent, you'll be in my store inside a month. Every apartment on Elm and Grand has the same kitchen tap, and it drips. Where are you living?
choice2: Is it really the same tap?
choice3: I'll come by if it drips.

line: Same tap, same washer, eighty cents. Look, I've sold that washer to three generations of tenants. The landlords buy the cheapest tap there is.
choice1: Has the store always been there?
choice2: Do you ever need help at the store?
choice3: Good to know. See you, Frank.

line: My grandfather opened it in 1951, my dad had it after him, and I've had the keys since '94. My nephew after me, if he ever learns to count change.
choice1: Where did your grandfather come from?

line: Calabria. Came over with eleven words of English, my dad used to say. By the time my dad was born he had the store and the English, and that was that. $ Look, nobody handed him anything. He just got on with it.
choice3: See you at the store, Frank.

line: _laughs a little_ The swear words. My dad made sure that's all we got. He didn't want us sounding like the old neighbourhood. $ [neutral] Anyway. You need a washer, you come see me.
Bother me? No. What would I do with it, sell hammers in it? _looks at his hands_ My grandmother used to sing something in the kitchen. I couldn't tell you what it was about.
choice2: See you at the store, Frank.

line: It was. And he did it so we wouldn't have to. That's my whole advice to anybody new: show up, sound like you're from here, and the town opens up. Took my family one generation. It can take you less.
choice1: Some people want to keep both.

line: At home, sure, speak whatever you want. English at the counter, that's all I ask. I've hired forty kids in thirty years, and the ones who sound like they're from here get the call back. I'm telling you what I've seen.
choice1: Fair. You've seen a lot of kids.
choice2: A kid can sound like two places.

line: Ha. Not this week. But in June I hire two kids for the summer. Stocking, the key machine, bags of salt in January if they last that long. You know anybody?
choice1: Maybe. What do you look for?

line: Look, they show up on time and they talk to the customer. That's it. I had a kid last year, smart as anything, but he'd mumble at old Mrs. Kowalski and she'd walk out. You have to talk like you want the sale.
choice1: And if their English isn't great yet?

line: Flu shot. My wife's idea. Frank DeLuca, the hardware store on Fifth. You waiting on somebody too?
Twenty minutes so far. I left my nephew alone at the register, so I'm losing money by the minute. You live around here?
Then you've got the tap that drips, right? Everybody on that block has it. Bring me the old washer and I'll match it.
Saturdays, yes. Weekdays it's contractors at seven and then the old guys who come in to talk about bolts. I like the old guys.
choice1: Has the store always been yours?

line: Frank is on a waiting-room chair with a clipboard on his knee. "Blood pressure. Every six months, my wife's orders. Forty questions and nowhere to write 'fine.'"
choice3: I'll let you fill it in.

line: 'Fine,' in the margin, all the way down. Look, the girl at the desk asked me twice if I wanted the form in another language. _taps the clipboard_ Me. Third generation. $ I guess she asks everybody. Fair enough, it's a clinic. At my counter it's English, but nobody ever died of the wrong washer.
choice2: Has the store always been yours?

line: Returning my wife's mysteries. She reads one a day and blames me for the late fees. You use this place much?
Good. Look, I tell every kid I hire: get a library card. Free computers, free newspapers, and the lady at the desk will fix your résumé if you ask nice.

Dana, Ruth, all of them. Ruth keeps asking me to sponsor her potluck. Look, everybody on this side of town ends up doing what Ruth asks, so I'll write the check. I told her I'll sponsor anything with a scoreboard.

The DeLuca Hardware Hornets. Under-twelves. That's what I really sponsor. The parents in the stands speak, what, six languages. On the field it's one. 'Run!' $ That's what I like about it. Nobody on that field cares where your parents came from.
choice1: Maybe I'll come to a game.

line: Returning my wife's mysteries. She reads one a day and blames me for the late fees. You use this place much?
Good. Look, I tell every kid I hire: get a library card. Free computers, free newspapers, and the lady at the desk will fix your résumé if you ask nice.

Dana, Ruth, all of them. Ruth came to the merchants' breakfast to ask for potluck money. Stood up, made her pitch. Half the room looked at me before they reached for their wallets. $ So I wrote a check, and they wrote theirs. Look, a potluck's not my kind of thing, but Ruth's all right.
choice1: So what do you sponsor, then?

line: Morning. A kid came into the store yesterday asking for 'the thingy for the faucet.'
choice1: Did you know what he meant?

line: Of course. Aerator. Thirty years of practice. His mom was out in the car and sent him in. He was maybe twelve, doing all the talking for her.

Every week. The kid talks, the mom pays. Look, I get it. My dad did that for his father at the bank. $ [guarded] He hated it. That's why he never taught us any of the old stuff. He didn't want us standing at a counter like that.
Never said so. He said, 'You're American, you talk like an American.' So I did. My kids do. _shrugs_ I don't know what he'd say about regret. We didn't talk like that, either.
Hey. You know what I like about you? You don't make a production of anything. You just show up.
choice2: What do you mean, a production?

line: I mean you come in the store, you say good morning, you know what you need. Some people want me to know their whole story before they buy a hammer. I just want to sell them the hammer.
choice1: Maybe they want you to know who they are.

line: Look, I'll know who they are. Give it a year and I'll know their kids' names. My grandfather didn't make anybody learn where Calabria was. He learned where Fifth Street was.
choice2: Where I'm from isn't a production, Frank.

line: The Fifth Street merchants do a breakfast, first Friday. Bagels, bad coffee, the city's parking guy. I'd like you there.
We complain about parking for an hour and then somebody mentions a job. Half the kids I know got hired that way. You'd meet the dry cleaner, the bank manager, the diner. You'd be good for us.
You're turning into a regular around here. Come to the merchants' breakfast Friday. I'll introduce you as my friend. Better than a résumé.
Because you show up and you talk to people. Look, that's ninety percent of it. The other ten is a good handshake, and we can work on that.
Afternoon. Excuse me, I'm in a mood today.
Two agents came into the store Tuesday asking about a kid who used to sweep for me. Polite. Badges, a photo.
choice2: Did they say what they wanted?
choice3: That's rough. I'll let you be.

line: What I know. He's a good worker, he showed up on time, he left in March. That's all I know and that's all I said. _rubs his jaw_ I don't ask the kids for more than a Social Security card. Maybe I should. I don't want to.
choice3: I'll let you get back to it.

line: Because he was sixteen and he swept better than my nephew. Look, I believe in rules. I also had his mother in on Saturday, buying a new lock for her door. I didn't like selling it to her.
Hey. You heard about the checkpoint out on Route 9? Don't let it worry you.
Look, people who follow the rules have nothing to fear. My grandfather came through with his papers and waited his turn. Nobody ever had to come looking for him.
choice1: It isn't that simple for everyone.

line: Maybe not. But you? You're fine. You're at the library, you're on Fifth, you talk like you're from here. You're basically from here. Nobody's stopping you on Route 9.
choice1: And if I weren't 'basically from here'?

line: _rubs his jaw_ Then you'd want your paperwork in order, same as anybody. I'm not saying it's nice. I'm saying it's the rules, and the rules were the rules for my grandfather too.
choice1: They weren't the same rules, Frank.

line: Afternoon. Before you ask, yes, I saw the news about Route 9.
choice1: What do you make of it?

line: I think it's a shame for his family. And I think the law's the law. Look, my grandfather did it the right way, and people who follow the rules have nothing to fear. That's not complicated.
choice1: The right way isn't open to everyone.

line: Maybe it's harder now. I'll give you that. $ But I'm not going to stand at my counter and say the rules don't matter. I've hired forty kids who did it by the book. What do I tell them?
choice1: Tell them the man on Route 9 was going to work too.

line: Haven't seen you on Fifth in a while. Somebody said you're at {homeCenter} most days.
No problem. They asked me to their {homeFestival} thing. I sent two folding tables. That's my contribution. I don't go to that kind of thing.

Look, it's nice. It's just not here, is it? Signs in four languages, a festival and a grant for everybody, and nobody asks anybody to be American anymore. $ If you came to America, why not become American? That's all my grandfather did.
Sure. At home. _shrugs_ My dad used to say both is how you end up neither. Maybe he was wrong. He was wrong about a lot. He was right about the store.
choice1: Come to the next festival, Frank.

line: The city wants signs in four languages now. In my store.
Safety stuff. The exits, the paint thinner, the key machine. Fine, I'll put them up. I'm not going to argue with a fire inspector.
But I'll keep telling people the counter runs in English. It runs faster. The kid who learns 'galvanized' this year is running a crew in five.
choice1: Signs won't slow the counter down.

line: Maybe not. My wife says I'm the only man on Fifth fighting a sign. _shrugs_ She also says I'd have hated being my grandfather in that store. She's probably right.
Haven't seen you on Fifth in a while. Somebody said you're over on Grand most days.
Sure, sure. Good people over there, they buy a lot of folding chairs. Look, just don't get stuck in one corner of town. That's my advice.
choice1: Grand is part of town, Frank.

line: It is. I'm just saying. My grandfather's first street had its own bakery, its own church, its own club. The guys who stayed on that street, their kids are still on that street. He moved to Fifth.
Ellen in 4C says you fixed her radiator valve. With a part from my store.
She tells everybody everything. Look, that's how you get known around here. Not a résumé. Somebody's radiator. In a year people will say you've always been here.
choice1: I'd still be from where I'm from.

line: Sure. Nobody's taking that. I'm just telling you what they'll say. _shrugs_ They said it about my grandfather too, at the end. Nobody on Fifth remembered he talked funny.
choice1: Did he want them to forget?

line: Morning.
choice1: Frank, about last time. No hard feelings?

line: None. I've had customers throw a wrench at me. You didn't throw a wrench.
Can't talk, I left the new kid alone at the register. Last time he sold a man forty feet of chain for the price of four.
